title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Images Are Big



Property
Value




Width × Height
224 × 224 pixels


Colour channels
3 (red, green, blue)


Total numbers
150,528


Weights in first layer (256 neurons)
~38 million




A standard fully connected network applied to images would have an enormous number of weights
Most of those weights would learn nothing useful, there is too much to learn from too little signal



A 224×224 colour image is over 150,000 numbers
A single fully connected layer with 256 neurons would have ~38 million weights
Training those weights reliably requires an enormous amount of data
A standard network cannot exploit the fact that an edge at (100,100) is similar to one at (101,100)

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
No Sense of Space






graph LR
  p1["pixel at 100,100"] --> N["neuron"]
  p2["pixel at 100,101"] --> N
  p3["pixel at 200,100"] --> N
  p4["pixel at 224,224"] --> N








A fully connected network treats every pixel as equally related to every other pixel
But nearby pixels carry related information, distant pixels do not
Images have spatial structure that standard networks are blind to





Fully connected networks receive every pixel with no information about which are neighbours
Images are not collections of independent numbers, they are spatially structured
A network that exploits spatial structure learns far more efficiently from far less data
CNNs are designed to do exactly this

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
A Sliding Window





graph LR
  img["Image: 224 x 224"] --> conv["Filter slides<br/>across image: 3 x 3"] --> fm["Feature Map:<br/>where is the pattern?"]







A filter (also called a kernel) is a small grid of weights (e.g. 3x3)
It slides across every position in the image
At each position, multiply the overlapping pixels by the filter weights, sum them up
The result is a feature map showing where the pattern was detected



Instead of connecting every pixel to every neuron, a small filter (e.g. 3×3) slides across the image
At each position, compute a weighted sum of the overlapping pixels
Output is a feature map, each value shows how strongly the pattern appeared at that position
One filter produces one feature map; a layer applies 32, 64, or 128 filters simultaneously

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
One Filter, One Pattern



Filter
What it detects
Feature map shows




Filter A
Horizontal edges
Horizontal boundaries in the image


Filter B
Vertical edges
Vertical boundaries


Filter C
Bright spots
Regions of high local brightness




Each filter learns to detect one specific pattern
A layer with 64 filters produces 64 feature maps — 64 different “views” of the image
The network learns which filters are useful during training



Filters are not hand-designed, the network learns them from data
Before training — Random; after training: detect patterns useful for the task (vessel edges, brightness gradients)
The number of filters per layer is a design choice — more filters, more patterns detected, more computation

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Simple to Complex

We saw this feature hierarchy in the previous session. Convolution is the mechanism that produces it.




Layer depth
Typical features detected




Layer 1
Edges, colour gradients, brightness changes


Layer 2
Corners, curves, short line segments


Layer 3
Textures, shapes, repeating patterns


Layer 4+
Complex structures, object parts, semantic features




Each layer builds on the feature maps of the layer before it
Complexity increases with depth automatically, through training



The hierarchy is not programmed, it emerges as the most efficient way to represent the data
Early layers — Low-level features (edges, gradients, colour transitions)
Middle layers — More complex patterns (shapes, textures)
Late layers — High-level, semantically meaningful features
For retinal images — Early = vessel edges; middle = vessel branching; late = global disease indicators

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
What a Trained Network Detects





graph TD
  A["Blood vessel edges<br/>(early layers)"] --> B["Vessel branching<br/>patterns"]
  C["Lesion boundaries<br/>(early layers)"] --> D["Lesion shape<br/>and density"]
  B --> E["Global disease<br/>indicators (late layers)"]
  D --> E
  E --> F["Disease / No disease"]








This diagram is approximate, the network discovers this structure; we cannot fully interpret every neuron
Broad pattern: early features are local and simple, late features are global and complex
Tools like Grad-CAM can visualise which parts of a retinal image the network focuses on
Typically, optic disc, vessel branching points, and regions with visible lesions

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Downsampling the Feature Map





graph LR
  fm["Feature Map: 224 x 224"] --> pool["Max Pooling:<br/>2x2, stride 2"] --> small["Smaller Map: 112 x 112"]







Max pooling — Divide the feature map into small regions, keep the maximum value from each
Halves the spatial dimensions with a 2×2 pool, stride 2
Keeps the strongest signal, discards fine spatial detail



Max pooling — Divide the feature map into 2×2 regions, keep only the maximum value from each
Result — Feature map half the width and height of the input
Reduces computation in subsequent layers and retains only the most salient features
Applied after each conv layer — Spatial dimensions shrink, number of channels grows

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Small Shifts Do Not Matter

If the pattern moves a few pixels, the max-pooled value stays roughly the same
The network does not need to see the same pattern in exactly the same location to recognise it
This is called translation invariance, it is critical for real-world images


A blood vessel does not need to be centred in the image to be detected.



In real datasets, the same structure appears at different positions across images
Without pooling: the network would need separate detectors for every possible position
Pooling generalises across positions, if the pattern appeared anywhere in the 2×2 region, it is preserved
A blood vessel at any position in a retinal image will still be detected

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Stacking Convolutional Blocks





graph LR
  img["Input:<br/>224x224x3"] --> b1["Conv Block 1:<br/>Conv, ReLU, Pool<br/>→ 112x112"] --> b2["Block 2:<br/>→ 56x56"] --> b3["Block 3:<br/>→ 28x28"] --> b4["Block 4:<br/>→ 14x14"] --> head["FC Head:<br/>Classification"]







Each block — Convolution → Activation (ReLU) → Max Pooling
Spatial dimensions shrink with each block
Number of channels (filters) grows: 3 → 32 → 64 → 128 → 256



Standard block: Conv → ReLU → Max Pooling, stacked repeatedly
Each block halves spatial dimensions and deepens the channel dimension
After 4 blocks: 14×14 spatial, 256 channels, each representing a complex pattern
A fully connected head then converts the feature maps to a class prediction

title: Deep Learning Without Math
section: The Baseline CNN in This Project
text:
The Baseline CNN in This Project





graph LR
  A["Input<br/>224×224, 3ch"] --> B["Conv Blocks ×4<br/>32→64→128→256ch"] --> C["AvgPool<br/>1×1, 256-dim"] --> D["FC Head<br/>256→128→2"] --> E["Disease /<br/>No disease"]







Four convolutional blocks, each building on the features of the last
Adaptive average pooling collapses spatial dimensions regardless of input size
Two fully connected layers with dropout for regularisation



Each block follows Conv2d → BatchNorm2d → ReLU → MaxPool2d
Channels grow: 3 → 32 → 64 → 128 → 256
Adaptive average pooling always produces a 256-dim feature vector regardless of input size
FC head maps to two output scores: healthy vs disease

title: Deep Learning Without Math
section: Why CNNs Are a Natural Fit
text:
Why CNNs Are a Natural Fit







Property
Why it matters for retinal images




Spatial structure
Vessel patterns and lesions are spatially localised


Translation invariance
Disease indicators appear anywhere in the image


Feature hierarchy
From vessel edges to global disease patterns


Parameter efficiency
~5,700 training images, far fewer than needed for fully connected





Fundus images have clear spatial structure: circular optic disc, radial vessels, localised lesions
CNNs are designed to exploit exactly this kind of structure
Translation invariance handles variation in field-of-view and image alignment across datasets
With only ~5,700 training images, CNN parameter efficiency is not a luxury, it is a necessity

title: Deep Learning Without Math
section: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants
text:
Standing on the Shoulders of Giants









ImageNet training
Fine-tuning for retinopathy




Images
1.2 million
~5,700


Categories
1,000
2


Training time
Weeks (on specialist hardware)
Hours (on a laptop)


What is learned
Rich general visual features
Task-specific adaptations




We start with a network already trained on ImageNet
Its weights already encode a sophisticated understanding of visual patterns
We then adapt those weights to our specific task



Training a network from scratch on ImageNet takes weeks on specialist hardware
The pre-trained weights encode rich, general-purpose visual features useful for many tasks
Instead of repeating this for every task, we start with pre-trained weights and adapt them
With ~5,700 images, this is not just convenient, it is often the only practical path to a good model

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Pre-Trained Weights Encode General Vision





graph LR
  imagenet["1.2M images:<br/>ImageNet, 1000 categories"] --> pretrained["Pre-trained<br/>ResNet-18"] --> finetune["Fine-tuning on<br/>retinal images"] --> classifier["Retinopathy<br/>classifier"]







ResNet-18 — 18-layer deep network, pre-trained on ImageNet
We replace only the final layer (1,000 categories → 2 categories)
Everything else—17 layers of learned visual features—is kept and adapted



ResNet-18 — 18-layer network with residual connections (shortcuts that stabilise training of deep networks)
Pre-trained on ImageNet; we replace only the final classification layer (1,000 → 2 categories)
The rest of the network—17 layers of learned visual features—is kept and adapted, not discarded

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Universal vs Task-Specific Features








Location
What is learned
Strategy




Early layers
Edges, curves, textures — universal
Keep — these transfer to any vision task


Middle layers
Shapes, patterns — partially universal
Lightly adapt


Late layers
Task-specific, high-level features
Fully retrain — adapt to retinopathy





Early layer features (edges, curves, textures) appear in retinal images just as in photographs of cats and cars
Discarding and relearning these from scratch would be wasteful
Late layers encode ImageNet-specific features (cars, dogs, birds) (less useful for retinopathy)
Strategy — Keep early layers, retrain late layers guided by retinal image data

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
The Two-Phase Fine-Tuning Strategy





graph LR
  A["Pre-trained ResNet-18<br/>(backbone frozen)"] -->|"Phase 1:<br/>5 epochs, lr = 1e-3"| B["Head stabilises,<br/>backbone unchanged"] -->|"Phase 2:<br/>up to 30 epochs, lr = 1e-4"| C["All layers<br/>fine-tuned"]







Phase 1 — Train only the new classification head — the backbone is frozen
Phase 2 — Unfreeze everything and train the whole network at a lower learning rate
You will see exactly this two-phase pattern in the code during Session 4



Unfreezing everything immediately risks large, noisy gradients from the random head corrupting pre-trained weights
Phase 1: train only the head — let it stabilise before it influences the backbone
Phase 2: unfreeze everything, train at a much lower learning rate — nudge rather than overwrite
This is the exact approach used in the notebook

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
The Bigger Picture

A CNN doesn’t look at every pixel at once — a small filter slides across the image, detecting one pattern at a time, which is why CNNs work so well with limited data.
The feature hierarchy — edges, then shapes, then structures — isn’t programmed in; it emerges because that’s the most efficient way to represent the data.
Weights trained on photographs of cats and dogs already encode a sophisticated understanding of visual structure; adapting them to retinal images takes hours, not weeks.

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Sessions

Session 1: Neural Networks
The core concepts behind deep learning: neurons, weights, layers, activation functions, the forward pass, loss functions, and how gradient descent trains a network.


Session 2: CNNs & Transfer Learning
How convolutional networks process images, the feature hierarchies they learn, and how pre-trained ImageNet weights can be adapted to new tasks with limited data.

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
A Step Change

In traditional machine learning, humans design the features the model uses
In deep learning, the model learns which features matter directly from data


The gap closed in 2012: one model changed the trajectory of an entire field.



In 2012, AlexNet entered the ImageNet competition and cut the top-5 error rate nearly in half
Not an incremental improvement — a signal that the rules had changed
Given enough data and compute, networks can learn to see in ways that surpass hand-crafted approaches
Every image recognition system today traces a line back to this moment

The step change happened in 2012, and has not stopped since.



2010–2011: modest, incremental gains, the kind researchers expected

Once the approach was validated, progress accelerated rapidly and has continued to do so

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
The Building Block





graph LR
  x1["x1 (input 1)"] -->|"x w1"| S["sum"]
  x2["x2 (input 2)"] -->|"x w2"| S
  x3["x3 (input 3)"] -->|"x w3"| S
  S --> A["activation function"]
  A --> out["output"]







Takes in several inputs
Multiplies each by a weight (its importance)
Passes the weighted sum through an activation function



A neuron takes several inputs, multiplies each by a weight (its importance), and sums them up
The weighted sum passes through an activation function — output is a single number
This is the building block; everything in deep learning is built from variations on this
The maths matters more than the biological metaphor

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Weights Are the Memory



Input
Weight
Interpretation




Bright region near disc
0.9
Strongly relevant


Overall image brightness
0.1
Weakly relevant


Background noise
0.01
Almost irrelevant




The weights are learned during training, they start random
A high weight: “this input matters for this decision”
The network’s knowledge lives entirely in its weights



Before training, weights are random, the network knows nothing
After training, weights encode what the network has discovered about inputs and outputs
“Learning” means weights have settled into values that produce good predictions
The weights are the model — save the weights, save everything the network knows

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Stacking Neurons



Each layer is a collection of neurons
Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer
Each layer passes a transformed signal forward







graph LR
  subgraph Input
    i1((i1))
    i2((i2))
    i3((i3))
  end
  subgraph Hidden
    h1((h1))
    h2((h2))
    h3((h3))
    h4((h4))
  end
  subgraph Output
    o1((o1))
    o2((o2))
  end
  i1 --> h1
  i1 --> h2
  i1 --> h3
  i1 --> h4
  i2 --> h1
  i2 --> h2
  i2 --> h3
  i2 --> h4
  i3 --> h1
  i3 --> h2
  i3 --> h3
  i3 --> h4
  h1 --> o1
  h1 --> o2
  h2 --> o1
  h2 --> o2
  h3 --> o1
  h3 --> o2
  h4 --> o1
  h4 --> o2









Many neurons together form a layer; stacked layers form a network
Each layer takes the previous layer’s outputs and applies a transformation via weights and activations
The cascade of transformations builds progressively complex representations of the input

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
What Each Layer Represents



Layer
Role




Input
Raw data — pixel values, numbers


Hidden
Learned representations — patterns, features


Output
The prediction — class probabilities




Hidden layers are named because we do not directly control what they learn
They discover useful structure in the data on their own



Input layer receives raw data (for images, pixel values) no transformation applied
Hidden layers build progressively more abstract representations of the input
Output layer converts those representations into a prediction (class probabilities)
Called “hidden” because their representations are not directly interpretable — learned, not designed

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Without Activation: Just a Line

A neural network with no activation functions behaves like one big linear equation
No matter how many layers you add, the output is still a linear function of the input
You could replace a 100-layer network (without activations) with a single matrix multiplication



Without activations, stacking layers does nothing useful — each is just a linear transformation
The composition of linear functions is still a linear function
An entire deep network without activations could be collapsed to a single matrix multiplication
Linear functions cannot model the complex, non-linear patterns present in real data like images

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Non-Linearity Unlocks Complexity





graph LR
  sum["Weighted sum"] --> relu["ReLU:<br/>negative to 0,<br/>positive unchanged"] --> out["Output"]







Activation functions introduce non-linearity after each weighted sum
The most common today: ReLU — simple, effective, fast
With non-linearity, stacked layers can model functions of arbitrary complexity



ReLU returns zero for negative inputs, passes positive inputs through unchanged
Simple but enormously effective, the output is not a linear function of the input
Non-linearity means stacking more layers genuinely increases what the network can model

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
How a Prediction is Made





graph LR
  A["Pixel values"] --> B["Layer 1: simple patterns"] --> C["Layer 2: complex patterns"] --> D["Layer 3: task features"] --> E["0.87 disease / 0.13 healthy"]







Data enters at the input layer and flows forward through each layer
Each layer transforms the representation
The output layer produces the final prediction



Pixel values enter the input layer and flow forward through each hidden layer
Each layer applies a transformation, building a progressively richer representation
The output layer distills the representation into a prediction
One direction only, no loops (hence “forward” pass)

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
A Number for Each Class



Class
Raw score (logit)
Probability




No disease
0.55
13%


Disease
2.1
87%




The class with the highest raw score is the prediction
Scores are converted to probabilities using the softmax function
Everything the network has learned collapses into two numbers at the end



Output layer produces two numbers (logits), one for each class
Softmax converts logits to probabilities that sum to 1
Highest probability = the prediction
Everything—all layers, weights, and learned features—collapses into two numbers at the end

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
How Wrong Are We?



Prediction
True label
Loss




90% disease
Disease
Low — correct and confident


55% disease
Disease
Medium — correct but uncertain


20% disease
Disease
High — wrong and confident




After a forward pass, we have a prediction and the correct answer (the label)
The loss function turns the gap between them into a single number



The loss function takes the prediction and the correct label, returns a number summarising the error
Loss near zero: accurate prediction; high loss: wrong or uncertain
Cross-entropy loss penalises confident wrong predictions particularly heavily
Pushes the network to be appropriately certain only when it has good reason to be

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
A Landscape to Navigate





graph LR
  A["Random weights - high loss"] -->|"adjust weights"| B["Better weights - lower loss"] -->|"adjust weights"| C["Good weights - low loss"]







Every set of weights produces a different loss value
Training is the process of navigating towards the minimum
Think of it as finding the bottom of a valley in a very high-dimensional space



Every combination of weights is a point in a vast space, there is one dimension per weight
The loss function gives a number at each point: how wrong is the network here?
Training = moving through this space towards a region of low loss
The landscape has many local minima but gradient descent finds good solutions reliably in practice

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Gradient Descent





graph LR
  A["Random weights"] --> B["Forward pass:<br/>make a prediction"]
  B --> C["Calculate loss:<br/>how wrong?"]
  C --> D["Backward pass:<br/>how much did each<br/>weight contribute?"]
  D --> E["Nudge each weight<br/>to reduce loss"]
  E --> B







Each step nudges every weight a small amount in the direction that reduces loss
The size of each step is controlled by the learning rate



The gradient tells us whether increasing or decreasing each weight would increase or decrease the loss
Move each weight a small step in the loss-reducing direction, step size = learning rate
Repeat: forward pass → compute loss → nudge weights → repeat
After thousands of iterations, weights converge to values that produce low loss on new data

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Backpropagation: Sharing the Blame

After a prediction, the error signal travels backwards through the network
Each weight receives a signal: “you contributed this much to the error”
All weights are updated at once, efficiently


The network learns by repeatedly asking: “what would I need to change to do better next time?”



Backpropagation sends the error signal backwards through the network after a forward pass
Uses the chain rule to calculate how much each weight contributed to the loss
Gives the gradient for every weight in one efficient backward pass
In PyTorch, a single loss.backward() call does all of this automatically

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
Layers Build on Layers



Depth
What the network detects




Layer 1
Edges, intensity gradients, colour transitions


Layer 2
Corners, curves, simple textures


Layer 3
Shapes, repeating patterns


Layer 4+
Complex structures, object parts




This hierarchy emerges automatically from training, it is not programmed in
Each layer combines the features from the layer before into something more complex



Deep networks discover a feature hierarchy automatically, they are not programmed in
The structure emerges because it is the most efficient way to represent the training data
The same hierarchy appears across different networks trained on different datasets
Depth enables this: a shallow network can only represent simple mappings; depth builds abstraction

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
From Pixels to Predictions





graph LR
  A["150,528 pixel values"] --> B["Edges and colour gradients"] --> C["Vessel structure and textures"] --> D["Lesion patterns and global features"] --> E["Disease / No disease"]







The network discovers what to look for, features are not hand-engineered
The relevant features for retinopathy emerge from training on labelled images
This is what makes deep learning powerful on complex, high-dimensional data



Traditional ML: a domain expert decides what features to extract (vessel diameter, lesion count, etc.)
Deep learning: the network discovers what to look for automatically
Emergent features often outperform hand-crafted alternatives
Core promise: automatic, scalable feature learning directly from raw data

title: Deep Learning Without Math
text:
The Short Version

The network’s knowledge lives entirely in its weights — before training it knows nothing; after, the weights encode everything it has learned.
Learning is just repeated error correction: make a prediction, measure how wrong it was, nudge every weight slightly in the direction that reduces the mistake.
Depth is what transforms simple edge detectors into disease classifiers — each layer builds on the last, and the hierarchy emerges automatically from training.
